You are helping a user write SQL queries to a database. If something is not clear, you can ask the user to clarify what they need. The schema for the database being accessed is the following:
        
CREATE TABLE conductor (
    Conductor_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Name TEXT,
    Age INT,
    Nationality TEXT,
    Year_of_Work INT,
    UNIQUE (Conductor_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE orchestra (
    Orchestra_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Orchestra TEXT,
    Conductor_ID INT,
    Record_Company TEXT,
    Year_of_Founded REAL,
    Major_Record_Format TEXT,
    UNIQUE (Orchestra_ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Conductor_ID) REFERENCES conductor(Conductor_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE performance (
    Performance_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Orchestra_ID INT,
    Type TEXT,
    Date TEXT,
    Official_ratings_(millions) REAL,
    Weekly_rank TEXT,
    Share TEXT,
    UNIQUE (Performance_ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Orchestra_ID) REFERENCES orchestra(Orchestra_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE show (
    Show_ID INT,
    Performance_ID INT,
    If_first_show bool,
    Result TEXT,
    Attendance REAL,
    FOREIGN KEY (Performance_ID) REFERENCES performance(Performance_ID)
);

There isn’t a “famous” flag/column in this schema, so you’d typically interpret “famous conductors” as conductors who lead orchestras with high-rated performances (or many performances/shows).

Here are a few useful SQL options:

### 1) Conductors with the highest total official ratings (most “famous” by audience)
```sql
SELECT
  c.Conductor_ID,
  c.Name,
  SUM(p."Official_ratings_(millions)") AS total_ratings_millions
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY total_ratings_millions DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

### 2) Conductors with the most performances
```sql
SELECT
  c.Conductor_ID,
  c.Name,
  COUNT(*) AS performance_count
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY performance_count DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

### 3) Conductors with the single highest-rated performance
```sql
SELECT
  c.Conductor_ID,
  c.Name,
  p.Performance_ID,
  p.Date,
  p."Official_ratings_(millions)" AS ratings_millions
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
ORDER BY p."Official_ratings_(millions)" DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Which definition do you want to use for “famous”: highest ratings, most performances, highest attendance (from `show`), or something else?
Famous conductors should be those who have led several orchestras, not just one.

```sql
SELECT
  c.Conductor_ID,
  c.Name,
  COUNT(DISTINCT o.Orchestra_ID) AS orchestras_led
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o
  ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.Orchestra_ID) > 1
ORDER BY orchestras_led DESC, c.Name;
```

If you mean “several” as 3+ (instead of 2+), change the `HAVING` to:
```sql
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.Orchestra_ID) >= 3
```
Make sure to include conductors based on their past activities, not just one performance.

To base it on *past activity* (across all their performances), you can require both **multiple orchestras** and **multiple performances**:

```sql
SELECT
  c.Conductor_ID,
  c.Name,
  COUNT(DISTINCT o.Orchestra_ID) AS orchestras_led,
  COUNT(DISTINCT p.Performance_ID) AS total_performances
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o
  ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
LEFT JOIN performance p
  ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.Orchestra_ID) > 1
   AND COUNT(DISTINCT p.Performance_ID) > 1
ORDER BY orchestras_led DESC, total_performances DESC, c.Name;
```

If you want a stricter “past activities” threshold (e.g., 3+ performances), change the second condition, e.g. `COUNT(DISTINCT p.Performance_ID) >= 3`.
I want to see the names of the conductors that meet these criteria too.

This query returns the **conductor names** (and also shows how many orchestras and performances they have, to confirm they meet the criteria):

```sql
SELECT
  c.Name,
  COUNT(DISTINCT o.Orchestra_ID) AS orchestras_led,
  COUNT(DISTINCT p.Performance_ID) AS total_performances
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o
  ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
LEFT JOIN performance p
  ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.Orchestra_ID) > 1
   AND COUNT(DISTINCT p.Performance_ID) > 1
ORDER BY orchestras_led DESC, total_performances DESC, c.Name;
```

If you truly want **only the names**, use:

```sql
SELECT c.Name
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
LEFT JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.Orchestra_ID) > 1
   AND COUNT(DISTINCT p.Performance_ID) > 1
ORDER BY c.Name;
```
